4.65.m: Skanda said:
O pot-born [Agastya], the liṅgas around Jyeṣṭheśvara,
which number five thousand, fully bestow perfections upon the sages. // 1
To the north of Jyeṣṭheśa is the great liṅga Parāśareśvara;
by merely beholding it, flawless knowledge is obtained. // 2
Right there is the perfection-bestowing liṅga named Māṇḍavyeśvara;
a man never acquires bad thoughts from beholding it. // 3

4.65.s: liṃgaṃ ca śaṃkareśākhyaṃ tatraiva śubhadaṃ sadā ..
4.65.d: लिंगं च शंकरेशाख्यं तत्रैव शुभदं सदा ..
4.65.m: And the liṅga called Śaṅkareśa right there always bestows auspiciousness;
there Bhṛgunārāyaṇa grants all perfections to devotees. // 4
The liṅga named Jābālīśvara there grants great perfections;
a creature never goes to an evil state from beholding it. // 5
The excellent sun [image] was established there by the sage Sumantu;
by merely beholding it, the disease of leprosy is cured. // 6
There is the Bhairavī named Bhīṣaṇā, of fearsome form;
worshipped with devotion, she destroys all danger to the sacred field. // 7
There is a liṅga near the thighs that releases one from the bondage of karma;
served by men with devotion, it grants supreme perfection within six months. // 8
The liṅga Bhāradvājeśvara and the excellent liṅga Mādrīśvara:

4.65.s: ekatra saṃsthite dve tu draṣṭavye sukṛtātmanā ..9..
4.65.d: एकत्र संस्थिते द्वे तु द्रष्टव्ये सुकृतात्मना ..9..
4.65.m: these two, situated in one place, are to be beheld by a virtuous person. // 9
O pot-born [Agastya], right there is the liṅga installed by Āruṇi;
from serving that liṅga, one obtains all prosperity. // 4.2.65.10
There is the most charming liṅga named Vājasaneya;
from beholding it, men obtain the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice. // 11
The auspicious liṅga Kaṇveśvara, the liṅga Kātyāyaneśvara,
the liṅga Vāmadeveśvara, and also Autathyeśvara, // 12

the liṅga of Kumbhi of great religious merit, and likewise Kausumeśvara, // 13
Agnivarṇeśvara, and also Naidhruveśvara,
the great liṅga Vatseśvara, and Parṇādeśvara, // 14
the liṅga Saktuprastheśvara, and likewise Kaṇādeśa,
and another great liṅga there designated for Māṇḍūka, // 15
the liṅga Vābhraveyeśvara, and Śilāvṛttīśvara,
the liṅga Cyavaneśvara, and Śālaṅkāyanakeśvara, // 16
the liṅga Kaliṅdameśvara, the liṅga Akrodhaneśvara,
the liṅga Kapotavṛttīśa, Kaṅkeśa, Kuntaleśvara, // 17

Mataṅgeśa, Marutteśa, and likewise Magadheyeśvara, // 18

Jārudhīśa, Jaleśa, Jālmeśa, and Jālakeśvara: // 19

From remembering, seeing, touching, worshipping, bowing, and praising [them],

4.65.s: na jātu jāyate jaṃtoḥ kaluṣasya samudbhavaḥ ..
4.65.d: न जातु जायते जंतोः कलुषस्य समुद्भवः ..
4.65.m: no arising of taint ever occurs to a living being.
Of these auspicious liṅgas in the sacred Jyeṣṭhasthāna—
Skanda said:
What once happened there in Jyeṣṭhasthāna, O great sage,
that I will tell you; listen to that which destroys sin.
While the Great Lord was strolling freely there in Jyeṣṭhasthāna,
Śivā playfully sported in the amusement of a ball game out of sheer curiosity.
Displaying the agility of her limbs as they leapt up and bent low,
her eyes bewildered by bees delighted by the fragrance of her breath,
making the ground uneven with lovely garlands falling from her loosened braid of hair,
radiant with drops of water dripping from the leaf-drawings on her sweating cheeks,
enveloped in the splendor of her body emerging from the parting of her opening bodice,
her lotus-hands made exceedingly crimson from the striking of the bounding ball,
the moving tips of her creeper-like brows made to dance by her eyes following the ball,
Mṛḍānī, the Mother of the Universe, was indeed seen playing.
And she was lovely, [beheld] by two sky-roving sons of Diti
who were, as it were, glanced upon by imminent death,
named Vidala and Utpala, haughty through the boon of the Creator,
by whom the men of the three worlds had been deemed as straw through the power of their own arms.
Desiring to abduct the Goddess, afflicted by the odd-arrowed [Kāma],
the two quickly descended from the sky, adopting sorcery's illusion.
Assuming the forms of attendants, they came near to Ambikā;
she of exceedingly restless mind [noticed] those two of extremely wicked conduct.
They were recognized by the Omniscient One from the restlessness born of their eyes.
Then Durgā, the slayer of terrible foes, was glanced at by the God.
Understanding the sign of his eyes, she who forms half the body of the Omniscient One
then struck them both simultaneously with that very ball.
Though exceedingly strong, struck by the ball of the Great Goddess,
spinning round and round, the two wicked ones fell down,
like two ripe fruits from a palmyra tree shaken by the wind from the stalk,
or two peaks of a great mountain struck down by the thunderbolt.
Having struck down the two great Daityas bent on committing a heinous act,
the ball then turned into the form of a liṅga.
And that liṅga then received the name Kandukeśvara,
near Jyeṣṭheśvara, warding off all wicked beings.
He who listens filled with joy to the origin of Kandukeśa,
and the devotee who worships it—whence could there be sorrow or fear for him?
For human beings devoted to Kandukeśvara, freed from sin,
Bhavānī, the destroyer of fear, would always provide welfare and protection.

4.65.s: mṛḍānī tasya liṃgasya pūjāṃ kuryātsadaiva hi ..
4.65.d: मृडानी तस्य लिंगस्य पूजां कुर्यात्सदैव हि ..
4.65.m: Mṛḍānī indeed always performs worship of that liṅga;
right there is the presence of the Goddess Pārvatī, bestowing perfection on devotees.
By whomsoever the great liṅga Kandukeśa is not worshipped in Kāśī,
how could Śiva and Bhavānī grant them all desired things?
And that liṅga, Kandukeśvara, must be seen with exertion,
as it is supreme in repelling the multitude of all afflictions.
Even upon hearing the name of Kandukeśvara, the succession of sins
quickly reaches destruction, just as darkness does upon meeting the hot-rayed [sun].
Skanda said:
Listen, O fortunate one, to the account that took place near Jyeṣṭheśvara,
which indeed produces supreme wonder, O brahmin.
At Daṇḍakhāta, the great sacred ford that gives satisfaction to gods, seers, and ancestors,
while brahmins were practicing supreme austerity free from desire,
the wicked Daitya named Dundubhinirhrāda, maternal uncle of Prahlāda,
thought of a means, asking: 'How may the gods be easily conquered?'

4.65.s: kiṃ balāśca kimāhārāḥ kimādhārā hi devatāḥ ..
4.65.d: किं बलाश्च किमाहाराः किमाधारा हि देवताः ..
4.65.m: 'What is the strength of the deities, what is their food, and what is their support?'
Reflecting much and having ascertained the truth with certainty:
'Undoubtedly, the first-born [brahmins] are the cause here upon reflection,'
he then repeatedly made an effort to kill the brahmins.
Because gods are eaters of sacrifices, and sacrifices originate from the Vedas;
Those Vedas depend upon the brahmins; therefore, the strength of the gods rests upon the twice-born.
Certainly all the Vedas, together with Indra, have the brahmins as their foundation.
The gods derive their strength from the brahmins; there is no doubt about this.

4.65.s: brāhmaṇā yadi naṣṭāḥ syurvedā naṣṭāstataḥ svayam ..
4.65.d: ब्राह्मणा यदि नष्टाः स्युर्वेदा नष्टास्ततः स्वयम् ..
4.65.m: If the brahmins were destroyed, the Vedas would then perish of themselves.
When the sacred traditions have perished, sacrifices are destroyed.
When sacrifices meet with destruction, the gods are deprived of their food.
Powerless, they will be easily conquered; and once the thirty [gods] are overcome,
I alone shall become the revered lord of the three worlds.
I will seize all the inexhaustible riches of the gods;
I will enjoy endless pleasures in a kingdom free of thorns.'
Having so resolved, O sage, the evil-minded one reflected further:
'Where are the most numerous twice-born, immensely augmented by brahmic splendor,
accomplished in reciting the revealed scriptures, and endowed with the power of austerity?

4.65.s: bhūyasāṃ brāhmaṇānāṃ tu sthānaṃ vārāṇasī bhavet ..
4.65.d: भूयसां ब्राह्मणानां तु स्थानं वाराणसी भवेत् ..
4.65.m: Vārāṇasī must be the dwelling place of the majority of the brahmins.
Having destroyed them first, I shall then go to another sacred ford.
Wherever in the sacred fords and wherever in the hermitages
all the first-born reside, they shall be eaten by me all around.'
Having thus made a resolve suited to his race, Dundubhinirhrāda,
wicked in conduct and deceptive, reached Kāśī and began killing the twice-born.
Wherever the best among the twice-born went to gather firewood and kuśa grass,
there in the forest that evil-minded one devoured them all.
Then, so that no one would know, he would conceal himself again:
becoming a wild beast in the forest, and taking the form of an aquatic creature in a reservoir of water;
invisible in form, deceitful, and imperceptible even to the gods.
By day, intent on meditation, he would remain among the sages like a sage,
watching the entry and departure from the huts;
and at night, in the form of a tiger, he would devour many brahmins.
He carried them away in utter silence, leaving behind not even a bone.
In this manner, numerous brahmins were struck down by that wicked one.
Once, on the night of Śivarātri, a devotee in his own hut,
having performed worship to the god of gods, remained absorbed in meditation.
And that lord of daityas, Dundubhinirhrāda, arrogant with power,

4.65.s: vyāghra rūpaṃ samāsthāya tamādātuṃ matiṃ dadhe ..65..
4.65.d: व्याघ्र रूपं समास्थाय तमादातुं मतिं दधे ..65..
4.65.m: assumed the form of a tiger and resolved to seize him.
Seeing that devotee immersed in meditation, his mind fixed on Śiva,
having performed the placement of weapon mantras, he was unable to overpower him.
Then omnipresent Śambhu, Hara, perceiving his intent,
set his mind upon killing the daitya of wicked form.
Just as the tiger sought to seize [him], Hara appeared,
the three-eyed crest jewel of world-protection, his intellect skilled in guarding devotees.
Seeing Rudra approaching from the liṅga worshiped by his devotee,
the daitya grew in that very form to the size of a mountain.
As the dānava looked disdainfully at the omniscient one,
the latter seized him as he attacked and crushed him in an armlock.
Then the five-faced [Śiva] struck the tiger on the head with his fist.

4.65.s: sa ca tenaiva rūpeṇa kakṣāniṣpeṣaṇena ca ..71 ..
4.65.d: स च तेनैव रूपेण कक्षानिष्पेषणेन च ..71 ..
4.65.m: And in that very form, crushed by the armlock,
the tiger roared in extreme agony, filling heaven and earth.
Their minds suddenly shaken with trembling by that roar,
the ascetics gathered in the night, following the sound.
Beholding Īśvara there with the beast of prey pinned under his arm,
they all bowed low and praised Śarva with cries of 'Victory, victory!':
'O protector, O protector of the world, [you have saved us] from this dreadful affliction!
O Īśa, grant us your favor; remain right here, O teacher of the world,

4.65.s: anenaiva hi rūpeṇa vyāghreśa iti nāmataḥ .. 75 ..
4.65.d: अनेनैव हि रूपेण व्याघ्रेश इति नामतः .. 75 ..
4.65.m: in this very form, under the name Vyāghreśa!
O Mahādeva, protect this superior abode forever;
protect us who dwell in the sacred ford from other afflictions as well!'
Hearing their words, the moon-adorned god
said, 'So be it,' and spoke again: 'Listen, O best of the twice-born!

4.65.s: yo māmanena rūpeṇa drakṣyati śraddhayātra vai ..
4.65.d: यो मामनेन रूपेण द्रक्ष्यति श्रद्धयात्र वै ..
4.65.m: Whoever will behold me here in this form with faith,
I will certainly destroy the host of his afflictions.

4.65.s: etalliṃgaṃ samabhyarcya yo yāti pathi mānavaḥ ..
4.65.d: एतल्लिंगं समभ्यर्च्य यो याति पथि मानवः ..
4.65.m: The mortal who travels along a path after properly worshipping this liṅga,
How could fear arising from thieves, tigers, and the like befall him?
Having heard this story of mine, and remembering this liṅga in his heart,
a mortal entering battle attains victory; it cannot be otherwise.
Having spoken thus, the God of gods vanished into that liṅga.
Filled with wonder, the brahmins then departed in the morning just as they had come.
Skanda said:
From that time forward, O pot-born one, the liṅga named Vyāghreśvara,
situated to the north of Jyeṣṭheśa, removes fear when seen and touched.
Even the extremely cruel servants of Yama fear those who are devotees of Vyāghreśvara,
proclaiming, 'Victory! May you live!'
Hearing of the manifestation here of the liṅgas beginning with Parāśareśvara,
a person will not be smeared by the mire of heinous sins.
Listening attentively to the origin of Kaṃdukeśa and likewise the appearance of Vyāghreśa,
a person is never afflicted by afflictions.
The liṅga Uṭajeśvara, situated to the west of Vyāghreśa,
arose to protect devotees; by worshiping it, one becomes fearless.

4.65.s: iti śrīskāṃde mahāpurāṇa ekāśīti sāhasryāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ caturthe kāśīkhaṇḍe uttarārdhe parāśareśvarādiliṃgasaṃbhavonāma paṃcaṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ .. 65 ..
4.65.d: इति श्रीस्कांदे महापुराण एकाशीति साहस्र्यां संहितायां चतुर्थे काशीखण्डे उत्तरार्धे पराशरेश्वरादिलिंगसंभवोनाम पंचषष्टितमोऽध्यायः .. 65 ..
4.65.m: Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, named 'The Origin of the Liṅgas Beginning with Parāśareśvara', in the latter half of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa, in the fourth section of the venerable Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, in the collection of eighty-one thousand verses.

4.66.m:
Skanda said:
I shall tell you of the other liṅgas around Jyeṣṭheśvara;
hear, O tormentor of Vātāpi!
To the south of Jyeṣṭheśa is the auspicious liṅga of the apsarases;
right there is the apsarases' well named Saubhāgyodaka.
Having bathed well in the water of that well and beheld Apsaraseśvara,
neither a woman nor a man incurs misfortune.
Right there near the reservoir is the liṅga named Kukkuṭeśa;
from worshiping it, people's families multiply.
On the bank of the Jyeṣṭhavāpī is the auspicious liṅga Pitāmaheśvara;
having performed śrāddha there, a person grants delight to the ancestors.
To the southwest of Pitāmaheśa, one must carefully worship
the liṅga Gadādhareśvara, which grants complete satisfaction to the ancestors.
In the direction of the Puṇyajanas from the liṅga Jyeṣṭheśvara, O sage,
the liṅga named Vāsukīśvara is to be worshiped on all sides.
Ritual acts such as bath and giving at the Vāsukikuṇḍa there
remove fear of serpents for people through the power of Vāsukīśa.
He who bathes on Nāgapañcamī in the pool called Vāsuki
will have no contact with poison arising from serpents.
A pilgrimage should indeed be made there on Nāgapañcamī during the rains;
the serpents always remain well-pleased in his lineage as well.
To the west of that pool is indeed the liṅga Takṣakeśvara;
it is to be worshiped with effort, granting all perfections to devotees.
To the north of that, O sage, is the pool named Takṣaka;
having performed water rites there, one is not overcome by serpents.
To the north of that pool, constantly bringing welfare to the sacred field
and destroying the fear of devotees, is the Bhairava named Kapālī.
That great sacred field of the Bhairava grants perfection to practitioners;
mantras accomplished there attain success within six months.
There is the Caṇḍī Mahāmuṇḍā, who pacifies obstacles for devotees;
she should be worshiped with offerings, worship, and gifts to attain one's desired goals.
The best of men who undertakes her pilgrimage on the Mahāṣṭamī
becomes renowned, rich in sons and grandsons, and endowed with fortune.
To the west of Mahāmuṇḍā is the Catuḥsāgaravāpikā;
having bathed in it, one has bathed in all four oceans.
That place named Catuḥsāgara is very famous;
and there four liṅgas were established by the oceans.
Worshiped in the four directions of that reservoir, they burn away sin.
To the north of that is the great liṅga named Vṛṣabheśvara,
established out of his own devotion by the bull of Hara;
from seeing it, liberation arises for men in six months.
To the north of Vṛṣeśvara is [the liṅga] named Gandharveśvara;
to its east is Gandharvakuṇḍa. Having bathed there, the best of men,
having worshiped Gandharveśvara, given gifts according to his ability,
and gratified the ancestors and gods, rejoices with the gandharvas.
There is a nāga named Karkoṭa to the east of Gandharveśvara;
there is the Karkoṭavāpī and the liṅga Karkoṭakeśvara.
Having bathed in that reservoir, worshiped Karkoṭeśa,
and venerated the nāga Karkoṭa, a man is honored in the world of serpents.
For those who have seen the nāga Karkoṭa after offering water in that reservoir,
no poison, whether stationary or moving, penetrates their bodies.
To the west of Karkoṭeśa is [the liṅga] named Dhuṃdhumārīśvara;
from the worship of that liṅga, people have no fear born of enemies.
The liṅga Purūraveśvara is situated to its north;
it should be seen with effort, granting the fruit of the four goals of life.
In front of it is the liṅga worshiped by Supratīka, the world-elephant,
named Supratīkeśvara, which increases fame and strength.
A great lake named Supratīka shines before it;
having bathed there and seen that liṅga, one attains the state of a guardian of the directions.
There is a Mahāgaurī there named Vijayabhairavī;
situated at the northern gate for protection, she is to be worshiped for the attainment of desires.
On the charming bank of the Varaṇā, the two gaṇas Huṇḍana and Muṇḍana
protect the sacred field, stopping obstacles.
They should be seen with effort for the sake of freedom from obstacles in the sacred field;
having seen Huṇḍaneśa and Muṇḍaneśa there, one becomes happy.

4.66.m:
Skanda said:
O foe of Ilvala, listen attentively to a story
of the splendid event that happened previously on the charming bank of the Varaṇā. / 33
Once, seeing the king of mountains whose mind was delighted,
Menā, that devoted wife, remembered Umā, sighed, and spoke thus: / 34
Menā said:
Noble lord, I know no news whatsoever
of that Gaurī since the time of her wedding, O king of mountains. / 35
That god whose gait is like that of a bull, adorned with ashes and serpents,
whose home is the great cremation ground, who is clad in the quarters—where is he now? / 36
O beloved, those eight mothers that were seen, beginning with Brāhmī,
the little girls having their forms, I consider them to be causes of distress. / 37
To him, the one and only trident-bearer without a second, there is no one else;
therefore, O lord, let an effort be made to obtain news of her. / 38
At these words of his beloved, the mountain who was affectionate toward his child,
his voice failing with affection for Umā, spoke tearfully: / 39
The king of mountains said:
O Menā, I myself will go in search of her;
my love, afflicted by the fire of not seeing her, troubles me excessively. / 40
From the day that Gaurī departed from my home,
I consider, O Menā, that the goddess dwelling in the lotus has departed since then. / 41
O dear wife, my ears, which once drank the nectar of her conversation,
have since then, O mistress of my life, been capturing other sounds. / 42
Since she who was like the full moon to my eyes has become distant,
alas, the moonlight, which sustains life, torments and distresses me from that day. / 43
Having spoken thus, taking jewels and various garments,
the lord of mountains departed at the powerful rising of an auspicious lagna. / 44

4.66.m: “Whoever comes here to Kāśī and builds a single abode for Śiva, / by him the entire three worlds are truly provided with an abode. / By him great gifts have been duly given, / on auspicious occasions, to worthy recipients, with daughter[s], and with abundant faith. / Whoever, according to the measure of his wealth, from riches earned by righteousness, / has built a great abode for Śambhu, Lakṣmī will never abandon him. / He has performed austerities, even subsisting on withered leaves, / who, having reached Vārāṇasī, has built an abode for Śiva. / He has offered all the great sacrifices rich in every excellence, / who has built an abode for the God of gods in the Forest of Bliss.” / Thus having heard his command, his followers then / built an excellent temple before the night had passed away. / Meanwhile, the Śaileśvara liṅga was installed by the King of Mountains, / with a pavilion illumined by the glittering radiance of moonstone gems. / And he had an inscription engraved, with a garland of laudatory letters, / proclaiming his own supreme elevation surpassing even all mountains. / Then, at sunrise, having bathed in the pool of the Pañcanada, / the King of Mountains bowed to and worshipped the Lord of Time (Kālarāja), / and leaving a heap [of treasures] there, went swiftly all around / to his own abode, accompanied by all his mountaineers. / Then in the morning, seeing that lovely temple on the auspicious bank of the Varaṇā, / the two gaṇas, Huṇḍa and Muṇḍa, delighted, / came to inform the God who had not seen it before. / Seeing Mahādeva holding a mirror shown by Umā, / the two gaṇas bowed down on the ground like a stick with palms joined. / Having received permission by a brow's flick, they made this report: / “O God of gods, we do not know by what person of firm devotion / an exceedingly beautiful temple has been built on the bank of the Varaṇā. / It was not seen by the two of us until evening, [yet] was seen this very morning, O Lord!” / 4.66.m: He who knows the whole matter, omniscient, spoke as if unknowing: / “O daughter of the Mountain King, let us go to see that temple.” / Having spoken thus, the Lord went forth with the Daughter of the Mountain and his gaṇas, O sage, / having mounted a great chariot, eager to see the temple. / Then Giriśa beheld the temple on the bank of the Varaṇā, / exceedingly delightful in design, built in the span of a single night. / Having descended from the chariot, he entered the sanctum sanctorum / and saw the great liṅga made of moonstone, / blazing with radiance, resembling the sprout of the glory of liberation, / producing purity of vision and cutting off rebirth. / While Īśvara was wishing to know, “By whom was this liṅga installed?”, / he saw before him the inscription indicating its maker. / Having read it slightly, as it were, the Destroyer of Kāma in his mind / said: “O Goddess, by good fortune! Behold your father's work!” / Hearing this, Umā was overjoyed, bearing on her limbs / the beauty of a kadamba flower, like the radiance of sprouts of joy. / Then the goddess made a petition to the God, having bowed at his feet: / “O Lord, you must dwell in this supreme liṅga day and night. / Whoever are devotees of this liṅga, Śaileśa the Great Lord, / to them you must grant great prosperity here and in the hereafter.” / Having said “So be it,” the God again spoke to that Pārvatī: / “By those who have bathed in the Varaṇā and worshipped Śaileśa, / and having gratified the ancestors with joy and given gifts according to their capacity, / there is no return for them here on the path of saṃsāra. / I shall dwell perpetually in the Śaileśvara great liṅga, O auspicious one; / I shall grant supreme liberation to the people who worship this liṅga. / Those who see Śaileśvara on the auspicious bank of the Varaṇā, / living in Kāśī, sorrow will not overcome them.” / A boon was also given by Umā at that liṅga, O Pot-born [Agastya]: / “Those who are devotees of Śaileśvara are my sons, without a doubt.”

Listen, best of munis, who checked the growth of the Vindhya mountains!
Ratnacūḍa, too, a self-controlled man, daily by way of the stepped-well,
having arrived from the world of the Nāgas and bathed in the water of the Mandākinī,
worshipped Ratneśvara with eight handfuls of jewels,
and joyfully offered eight golden lotuses.
Once, at the time of a dream, Ratneśa, bearing the form of a liṅga,

"The maiden whom you shall rescue, abducted by the dānava,
having conquered that dānava in battle, she shall be your wife."

having slain the dānava and freed that maiden by his own prowess,
brought her back to the earth from Pātāla by way of the stepped-well.

having worshipped the liṅga and also performed circumambulation,
as he came outside from the delightful hall of Ratneśa,

Īśvara said:
Of the liṅga Ratneśvara, which is my stationary form,
which bestows all things to all, the power is incomparable, O daughter of the mountain!
In this liṅga, thousands of perfected ones have attained supreme perfection.
This liṅga remained concealed until today, O slender-waisted lady!
By your father Himavat, who is devoted to me in every way,
Ratneśa was revealed by means of great gems acquired through merit.
My love for this liṅga is immense, O daughter of the king of mountains!
In Vārāṇasī this liṅga should be worshipped with earnest effort.
Various jewels are obtained through the grace of Ratneśa, O Umā,
as well as the jewel among women, the jewel among sons, and even heaven and liberation, my dear!

Agastya said:
Tell of the origin of Ratneśvara, O six-faced one, / the jewel-like great liṅga that is praised in Kāśī. 1
What is the greatness of this liṅga, and by whom was it established? / Explain this in detail, O delighter of Gaurī's heart! 2
Skanda said:
I will tell you the māhātmya of Ratneśvara, O sage, / and how the jewel-liṅga appeared on earth. 3
The mere name of which liṅga, when heard, destroys the sins / accumulated in three lifetimes—of its appearance I speak, O sage. 4

its sky enveloped in flames, illuminating the directions with radiance? / What is its name, what is its nature, and what is its power, O destroyer of mundane existence? 11

The God of gods said:

O lovely lady, by your father, the king of mountains Himavat, / for your sake a great hoard of jewels was brought here. 14

Whatever things are regarded as jewels in the three worlds, / a mortal obtains them all by worshipping Ratneśvara just once. 30
Those who, free from desires, will worship the liṅga Ratneśa, / shall all become my gaṇas and will see me here at the end. 31
Whatever reward is proclaimed for chanting the Rudras a crore of times, / that reward is obtained, O goddess, by worshipping Ratneśa. 32
And regarding this beginningless and eternally perfected liṅga, I will tell you what occurred: / a most wondrous legend that cuts away all sins. 33
Formerly, in this place, there was a dancing girl skilled in the arts of the stage; / once, in the month of Phālguna, on the night of Śivarātri, that Kalāvatī, 34
keeping vigil, danced and sang a lovely song; / and being skilled in instruments, she herself played diverse musical instruments. 35
Having thus delighted the great liṅga Ratneśvara / with that triple music, the actress went to her desired place. 36
Having succumbed to the law of time there, that excellent dancer / was born as the daughter of the Gandharva king Vasubhūti. 37
By the merit of that song, instrumental music, and gentle dance, / performed there before the Lord during the vigil on Śivarātri, 38
she was born charming, named Ratnāvalī, endowed with beauty and loveliness, / skilled in the whole array of arts, speaking with sweet melodies. 39
Ever bringing delight to her father, Vasubhūti, O pot-born [Agastya], / she was skilled in all Gandharva lore, a great mine of jewel-like virtues. 40
O sage, she had three female friends, receptacles of charming cleverness, / by name Śaśilekhā, Anaṅgalekhā, and Citralekhā. 41

In this way, observant of her vows, that foremost Gandharva daughter lived; / together with those friends of hers, she would see the liṅga constantly.
Once, having worshipped Ratneśa, this excellent liṅga of mine, / the young girl adored it with a charming garland of songs.
Her three friends also went, O Umā, to perform circumambulation of the liṅga; / pleased by her singing, I, abiding in the liṅga, became a grantor of boons:
'He who will take pleasure with you tonight, O Gandharva maiden, / having a name identical to yours, he shall become your husband.'
Drinking deeply of this nectar of words born from the ocean of the liṅga, / she became sluggish with an abundance of bliss, exceedingly bashful.
Then she went by the sky-path with her friends to her father’s home, / happily relating her tale before her companions.
Congratulated by those friends with cries of 'By good fortune! By good fortune!': / 'Today your desire will come to pass through the worship of Ratneśa.
If he who steals your maidenhood comes to you tonight, / that thief must be bound very firmly with the cords of your creeper-like arms,
so that that sole foundation of good deeds may be seen by us / tomorrow morning itself—your beloved, ordained by Ratneśa, who fulfills your wish.
While we had gone off rejoicing, you, through your deep modesty, / O! You have brought the Ratneśvara-liṅga before your very eyes!
O, the dawn of good fortune for mortals! O, the accumulation of merit! / For success comes only to one among those even standing together.
Those who speak of the supremacy of destiny speak the truth, not falsehood: / destiny alone bears fruit; neither effort nor other strength avails.
For you and for us there was indeed the very same effort, / but supreme destiny bears fruit for one, as for you, and not before us.
Such is the worldly way, spoken in the course of friendly talk; / yet the attainment of your wish is indeed clear to us.'

The friends said:
'He whose village is not known to us, nor his name, nor his lineage— / how is he to be found, auspicious one? What means may be employed?'
Having heard that speech of theirs full of doubt, Ratnāvalī said: / 'Friends, in securing him for me, you are dull—' and fainted.
With these half-spoken words, 'you are of blunted powers'— / that which was to be said by her, she uttered as 'you are dull'.
Then those friends swiftly applied many cooling measures / to banish her torment, in order to pacify her fainting.
When the fainting did not depart from those various cooling remedies, / then the ceremonial bath water of Ratneśa was brought by one [of them].
From its sprinkling, her faint ceased in that very instant; / as if awakened from sleep, she repeatedly uttered, 'Śiva, Śiva!'
Skanda said:
For his devoted ones endowed with faith, even in great affliction, / there is no other remedy whatsoever except the water from the Lord’s feet.
Even those diseases difficult to cure that reside outside or inside the body / are indeed destroyed through faithful contact with the Lord’s water, not otherwise.
He by whom the water from the Lord’s feet is constantly revered, / pure internally and externally, misfortune does not approach him.
Afflictions caused by other beings, or afflictions caused by the gods, / and likewise afflictions originating from oneself—the holy water from his feet removes them.
Then, her fever having departed, O sage, the Gandharva daughter, / discerning what was fitting, spoke to those friends with an affectionate and calm mind:

Seeing those serpents, even depicted in the painting, / the maiden felt for a moment as though she had enjoyed pleasure.
She looked at each one of the youths, all born in the lineage of Śeṣa, / likewise those belonging to Takṣaka's family, and then those sprung from the lineage of Vāsuki,

Ratnāvalī, observing silence out of modesty, / looked at Citralekhā with a sidelong glance, her lips trembling.
Anaṅgalekhā, looked at with a side-glance by Śaśilekhā, then / pulled away the border of the cloth that Citralekhā had thrown over it.

From the moment of seeing him, her vision was filled with tears of joy; / the surface of her cheeks was covered with droplets of sweat.
The slender creeper of her body trembled, wearing a bodice of horripilation; / she stood motionless for a moment with closed eyes, as if depicted in a painting.
Then Citralekhā, approaching her, consoled the agitated maiden: / "Do not be anxious, O Gandharva maiden; your wish has been granted today!

Then, as they were travelling along the path of the sky, by decree of fate / they were spotted by the Dānava Subāhu, who lived in the realm of Pātāla.
Seizing all four of them, the Dānava set out for his home, / like a lion with frightful fangs in his mouth [carrying off] female deer in the wilderness.
Seeing him with his face made terrible by fangs / and his eyes red with blood, those Gandharva maidens became abodes of trembling:
"Alas, Mother! Alas, Father, save us! Alas, Providence, do not ordain that / which has been begun—this extremely cruel act toward helpless girls!
Alas, Destiny! What have we done, unfortunate as we are? / Even mention of anything other than good deeds was never uttered in our hearts!
Leaving aside childish play, leaving aside the worship of Ratneśvara, / obedient to our parents with pure conduct, we know of no selfish desire!
Who here will rescue us poor girls, fallen into the netherworld, / devoid of a protector, seeking protection? O Śambhu, O Ratneśa, omnipresent one!"

4.67.m:
As the Gandharva daughters were thus lamenting in deep distress, / that high-minded king of Nāgas, Ratnacūḍa, heard them:
"Who is this taking the name of my lord Ratneśa, the great ruler, / the king of liṅgas who shatters the bonds of karma?"
Hearing once more the cry of distress uttered from the maiden's mouth— / "O Ratneśa, save us! Save us!"—he took up his weapon and went forth.
Ratnacūḍa beheld him, who from drinking the serum of fat / and consuming human flesh was behaving wicked and utterly frenzied.
And he rebuked him: "O wicked one! O abductor of virtuous maidens! / You have come within the range of my sight; where will you go now, O vile one?
Bereft of life by my arrows, make your journey, O evil-minded one, / toward the city of Vaivasvata, [for] my mind is resolved on protecting the afflicted!
Those by whom the name of Ratneśvara is uttered clearly, / even in the calamity of universal dissolution, have no fear of such as you, who are fear personified.
Indeed, for those men who have found protection in the great name of Ratneśvara, / whence can there be any fear of birth, old age, disease, or the age of Kali?"
Having spoken thus, he said, "Do not fear!" / to those maidens trembling with fright, whose eyes were fixed upon his face like deer smelled out by a tiger.
Having thus consoled the Gandharva maidens, that son of the serpent king / drew his bow up to his ear and discharged an arrow.
That king of Danus also, enraged like a serpent stepped on with a foot, / whirled around and hurled a huge iron club resembling the rod of Death.
For him in whose heart the Ratneśvara liṅga fully manifests itself, / even the rod of Death becomes like a wooden fire-brand.
With his great arrows he cut the iron club to pieces midway in the air, / just as a wicked person's lifespan is severed right midway in this world.
Then he shot an arrow at him, shining like the fire of cosmic dissolution; / that arrow entered his heart, searched it thoroughly,
and having driven out his vital breaths, returned of its own accord to the quiver.

4.67.m:
Having known in full the wickedness present in his heart, / the snake's arrow went forth as if to proclaim it before the maiden of the quarters.
He who wishes to enjoy happiness through wealth acquired unjustly— / that wealth departs, and how can he have life or happiness?
Having thus slain that Dānava, the mighty king of snakes / then answered those maidens: “Who are you, and whose daughters are you?
From where did you encounter this wicked one born of Danu? / Or where was the liṅga of Ratneśvara seen by you,
by uttering whose name's syllables your supreme danger vanished? / Tell that quickly, so that I may know it in truth.”
Having heard his words, filled with supreme love, / looking at each other's faces, [they said:] “Who can this be, seeming as if seen before?
Who is this friend without cause who has appeared in the wilderness, / by whom, having wagered his own life, we young girls were saved?
Just by the sight of him, though naturally fickle, / our senses have indeed become sluggish, as if having drunk ambrosia.
Our eyes do not dare to go elsewhere in any way, / even upon seeing another object that is yet more delightful.
Having abundantly attained the sweetness of the nectar of his speech, our ears / make no demand for grasping other sounds in their existence.
These feet of ours, though restless, have attained lameness / upon beholding this youth, the thief of the jewel of our virtuous minds.”
Speaking thus softly among themselves, / those young girls did not recognise him, though they had seen him in the painting.
Because of their extreme terror of the Dānava of terribly frightful form, / their vision had become blinded; those fawn-eyed girls did not recognise him.
And they said to that youth who had saved their lives: / “O noble one, as you have asked with a heart filled with affection,
we shall tell you everything; direct your mind [to us] for a moment.

4.67.m:
“This is the daughter of the Gandharva king Vasubhūti, / a maiden named Ratnāvalī, a great mine of jewels of virtues.
We are her companions, always following her like shadows.
Beginning even from childhood, having been permitted by her father, / she always went to worship the liṅga named Ratneśvara in Kāśī.
And a boon was given to her by that pleased Śambhu: / ‘He who will take away your maidenhood in a dream, O girl,
having a name equal to your own name, he shall be your husband.’ / Even after obtaining in a dream the youth who enjoyed her, she became exceedingly sorrowful,
and again she was severely tormented by the fire arisen from separation from him. / Then, by our artistic skill, he too was shown in a painting,
whose village, name, or family was not even known. / Having seen him even drawn in a painting, she revived again.
Then, having bowed to Ratneśvara, she was eager [to return] to her own home. / Going with her along the path in the sky over the wilderness,
an unexpected Yama seized us and entered Pātāla. / What happened after that, you yourself know concerning that lowest of Danu’s sons.
O noble one, thus has our own story been recounted by us. / Grant us your grace: who are you before us, O treasure of compassion?
And from the time that wicked Dānava was seen by us, / from that time our eyes have lost their luster, as if by lightning.
Fleeing in fear, O savior from danger, we truly know nothing at all: / where we are, who we are, who you are, what has happened, and what will be.”
Having heard this, that righteous young prince of snakes, / having comforted those terrified girls, whose mind was virtuous, said this:
“Come with me; I shall show Ratneśa to you.” / Calling them thus, he led them to a pleasure pond with pleasant waters,
with steps of diverse gems, resounding with geese and ruddy sheldrakes, / as if bidding welcome under the guise of the sounds of waterfowl.

4.67.m:
There, permitted by him, having plunged into the pleasure pond, / they then emerged again, dressed in garments, flowers, and ornaments.
Having come outside, looking around as if spellbound, / the Gandharva women, having beheld the abode of Ratneśa near Kālarāja,
then said to one another, as if astonished: / “Is this a dream, or is it true, or a sport of Ratneśvara?
Or are we ourselves bewildered? Are we not Gandharva women? / What is this? We do not know at all, like a magician's display!
This is clearly the north-flowing Gaṅgā here; / this is the pond of Śaṅkhacūḍa, and this is the dwelling of Śaṅkhacūḍa.
This is the Pañcanada sacred ford; this is the dwelling of Vāgīśvara, / just by the sight of which the power of speech expands.
And this is Śaṅkhacūḍeśvara, consecrated by Śaṅkhacūḍa, / by the sight of which men have no fear arising from the serpent of Death.
This is the oblong reservoir named Mandākinī, having sacred waters, / having offered water in which, mortals do not enter the world of mortals.
This is the goddess Āśāpurī, who was praised by the enemy of Tripura / on the auspicious bank of the Mandākinī when he desired to conquer Tripura,
who, worshipped even today by mortals, fulfills the hope of petitioners. / And to the west of Mandākinī is this Siddhyaṣṭakeśvara,
from whose worship the eight perfections would clearly be present in one’s home. / And right there is the pool named Siddhyaṣṭaka, with pure water,
having bathed in which and performed the śrāddha, one freed from dust would go to heaven. / And those eight perfections are forms which grant all perfections in Kāśī.
And this is the great king Vināyaka, the bestower of all perfections, / to whom when men bow down, obstacles perish.
That is the high, gold-resplendent palace of Siddheśvara, / with flags and banners of gems, from the sight of which perfection is attained.
In the middle part of the sacred field, this indeed is Madhyameśvara.”

4.67.m:
"By the sight of which one does not dwell between the middle world and the nether world.
Having worshipped Madhyameśa, a man becomes an emperor whose realm extends to the sea / in the middle world, and then attains liberation.
To the east thereof is the liṅga Airāvateśvara, bestower of desired perfections, / upon whose banner is seen the lovely elephant Airāvata.
This temple of Vṛddhakāleśvara is fashioned of gems, / wherein the moon with the host of stars dwells every new-moon night;
by the sight of which time has no power over men in this transmigratory existence, / Kali truly has no power, nor do heaps of sins."
While the maidens, as if bewildered, were talking thus, / Vasuvibhūti, that gandharva, came in haste,
having heard the news from Nārada about the son of Danu, Subāhu: / how his beloved daughter Ratnāvalī, together with her companions, was abducted
while returning from Ratneśvara through the empty path of the sky; / how he carried her to Pātāla, and how a battle then ensued;
how that son of Danu, Subāhu, was slain by the devotee of Ratneśa, / Ratnacūḍa, with a great bow and an arrow;
and how, having inquired of the matter, he brought [them] by way of the stepped-well, / that stepped-well of Śaṅkhacūḍa that opens into the nether worlds;
and how, having reached and emerged from it, the maidens, even upon seeing Kāśī, / fell into great bewilderment, gazing eagerly.
Seeing his daughter, who seemed as if born anew, / accompanied by her companions, the beauty of her lotus-face unfaded,
the king of the gandharvas embraced her, repeatedly smelled her forehead, / placed her on his lap, and respectfully asked about the whole account.
Then she related the story of her abduction by the Danu-born, / but omitted [mention of] Ratneśvara, the obtaining of the boon, and the dream-state.
Then, having discerned Ratnāvalī's intention through the expressions of her face, / Śaśilekhā recounted [everything] at length in clear words.

4.68.m: Hear another event that occurred there, O best of brahmins,
which produces great wonder and removes the gravest sins.
While Maheśvara was thus telling the story of Ratneśa,
there arose a great uproar on all sides: “Save us! Save us!”
This Gajāsura, the son of Mahiṣāsura, was approaching,
crushing all the Pramathas, arrogant with the intoxication of his own strength.

4.68.s: yatrayatra dharāyāṃ sa caraṇaṃ pramiṇoti hi ..
4.68.d: यत्रयत्र धरायां स चरणं प्रमिणोति हि ..
4.68.m: Wherever he set his foot upon the earth,
he made the mountains shake there under his weight.
By the velocity of his thighs, trees fell down together with mountain peaks;
by the blow of his staff-like arm, piles of rocks were pulverized.
From the friction of his crest, the clouds fled even from the sky,
and even today they have not shed their blackness born from contact with his bodily filth.
By the mass of his sighs, the great oceans rose in high waves,
and the rivers too surged with swift billows along with their great fish.
Nine thousand yojanas was the height,
and just as great was the width of the body of this sorcerer.
The tawny glow and also the tremulous flicker of his eyes
is not abandoned by lightning even today; this one came in haste.

4.68.s: yāṃyāṃ diśaṃ samabhyeti soyaṃ duḥsaha dānavaḥ ..

4.68.m: Whichever quarter this intolerable Dānava approached,
that quarter surely flattened itself out, as if from terror of him.
Having obtained a boon from Brahmā, he treated the three worlds like straw,
[thinking,] “I cannot be slain by women or men overcome by lust.”
Then, knowing the approaching bull of Daityas
to be invulnerable to anyone else, the trident-wielding Lord struck him with his trident.

regarding himself as if transformed into an umbrella, praised Hara.
Gajāsura said:
O trident-handed Lord of the gods, I know You as the destroyer of Smara.

I wish to make a small request; attend to what I say.
I speak the truth, not a falsehood, O Conqueror of Death; consider it.
You alone are worthy of worship by the worlds, standing above the universe;

4.68.m: and I am standing above You, so I have conquered!
I am blessed, I am favored, standing on the tip of Your trident.
All must die in the course of time; such a death leads to the highest good.

Śambhu, laughing, spoke to Gajāsura, O jar-born one:
Īśvara said:
O Gajāsura, I am pleased, O treasure-house of great valor!
Name a boon agreeable to you; I shall grant it, O intelligent Asura.
Hearing this, that lord of the Daityas replied to Maheśvara.
Gajāsura said:

4.68.s: yadi prasanno digvāsastadā nityaṃ vasāna me .. 4.2.68.20 ..
4.68.d: यदि प्रसन्नो दिग्वासस्तदा नित्यं वसान मे .. 4.2.68.20 ..
4.68.m: If You are pleased, O space-clad Lord, then wear forever
this hide of mine, O Virūpākṣa, purified by the fire of Your trident,
fitting Your own size, pleasant to the touch, wagered on the battlefield.
May it always have a pleasing scent; may it always be exceedingly soft;
may it always be spotless; and may it always be a splendid ornament.
Even after experiencing the flames of the fire of great austerity for a very long time, O Lord,
this hide of mine has not burned; therefore it is a treasury of holy fragrance.
O sky-clad one, if this hide of mine were not virtuous,
then how could its contact with your body have occurred upon the battlefield?

4.68.s: anyaṃ ca me varaṃ dehi yadi tuṣṭosi śaṃkara ..
4.68.d: अन्यं च मे वरं देहि यदि तुष्टोसि शंकर ..
4.68.m: Grant me also another boon, if you are pleased, O Śaṃkara:
starting from this day onward, may your name be Kṛttivāsas [‘clad in a hide’]!”

4.68.s: iti tasya vacaḥ śrutvā tathetyuktvā ca śaṃkaraḥ ..
4.68.d: इति तस्य वचः श्रुत्वा तथेत्युक्त्वा च शंकरः ..
4.68.m: Having heard his speech, Śaṃkara said, “So be it,”
and spoke again to that Daitya whose mind was made pure by devotion:
Īśvara said:
“Listen, O Daitya, treasury of merit, to another boon most difficult to obtain,
O you who abandoned your body in battle within the great sacred field of Avimukta!
May this virtuous body of yours, in this sacred field that brings about liberation,
become my liṅga here, granting liberation to all,
named Kṛttivāseśvara, destroying the greatest sins!
This supreme [liṅga] shall be the head of all liṅgas whatsoever.
As many liṅgas as there are in Vārāṇasī, even the greatest ones,
this one is supreme among them all, as the head is the foremost among the limbs.
For the welfare of human beings, I shall abide here together with my retinue.
When this liṅga is seen, worshipped, and praised in hymns,
a mortal becomes one who has accomplished his purpose and does not enter worldly existence again.
Rudras, Pāśupatas, Siddhas, seers who contemplate the reality,
peaceful, self-controlled, having conquered anger, free from dualities, devoid of possessions,

4.68.s: avimukte sthitā ye tu mama bhaktā mumukṣavaḥ ..
4.68.d: अविमुक्ते स्थिता ये तु मम भक्ता मुमुक्षवः ..
4.68.m: my devotees desiring liberation who reside in Avimukta,
indifferent to honor and dishonor, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal—
for their grace I will dwell in the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga.
A hundred million sacred fords, each and every day,
will come at the three junctures of the day to Kṛttivāsa; of this there is no doubt.
Men born in the Kali and Dvāpara ages whose minds are defiled,
destitute of good conduct, averse to truth and purity,
bound by deceit, hypocrisy, and greed, possessed of delusion and egotism,
brahmins who consume the food of Śūdras, gluttonous and excessively covetous,
their minds and intellects turned far away from twilight prayers, ritual ablutions, recitation of mantras, and sacrifices—
reaching Kṛttivāseśvara, freed from all sins,
they will attain liberation with ease, just as do the virtuous.

4.68.s: kṛttivāseśvaraṃ liṃgaṃ sevyaṃ kāśyāṃ tato naraiḥ ..
4.68.d: कृत्तिवासेश्वरं लिंगं सेव्यं काश्यां ततो नरैः ..
4.68.m: Therefore, the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga must be worshipped in Kāśī by men.
Liberation elsewhere is exceedingly difficult to obtain across thousands of other births;
at the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga, however, it is attained in a single birth.
Sin committed in a previous life, which might slowly perish
by means of austerity, charity, and the like, perishes instantly from the sight of the Lord of Kṛttivāsa.
The mortals who will worship the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga

4.68.s: praviṣṭāste śarīre me teṣāṃ nāsti punarbhavaḥ ..41..
4.68.d: प्रविष्टास्ते शरीरे मे तेषां नास्ति पुनर्भवः ..41..
4.68.m: have entered into my body; for them there is no rebirth.
One should reside here in Avimukta, recite the Śatarudriya,
and behold the god Kṛttivāseśvara again and again.
Whatever fruit is attained through the well-recited seven crores of Mahārudras,
that fruit is attained in Kāśī from the worship of Kṛttivāsas.
Fasting on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, one should stay awake through the night;
he who reverently worships the Lord of Kṛttivāsa shall attain the supreme goal.
He who celebrates a great festival on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra

4.68.s: kṛttivāseśvare liṃge na sa garbhaṃ pravakṣyete .. 45 ..
4.68.d: कृत्तिवासेश्वरे लिंगे न स गर्भं प्रवक्ष्येते .. 45 ..
4.68.m: at the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga will not enter another womb.”
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods took that hide,
the great [hide] of Gajāśura, and clothed himself in it, he whose garment was the quarters of the sky.
A great, great festival took place on that day, O jar-born one [Agastya],
on which the sky-clad god assumed the status of Kṛttivāsas.
Where the Daitya had been made into an umbrella, having planted the trident into the surface of the earth,
from pulling out that trident a very great pool was formed there.

4.68.s: tasminkuṃḍe naraḥ snātvā kṛtvā ca pitṛtarpaṇam ..
4.68.d: तस्मिन्कुंडे नरः स्नात्वा कृत्वा च पितृतर्पणम् ..
4.68.m: Bathed in that pool and having performed the libation to the ancestors,
having seen Kṛttivāseśvara, a man will have accomplished his purpose.
Skanda said:
“Hear what happened at that sacred ford, O Agastya:
crows turned into swans by the power of that sacred ford!
Once in the past, at Kṛttivāsa, there was a pilgrimage on the full-moon day of Caitra.
Food that had been presented as offerings was heaped up in piles there.
Seeing it, O brahmin, birds gathered in large numbers from temple priests.
Fighting with one another in the air for that food,
the emaciated crows were cawing harshly against those fattened by the offerings;
and the weak ones were struck with beaks by those powerful ones whose limbs were very well-nourished.
Being beaten, they fell down into that pool from the courtyard of the sky.
Saved by their remaining lifespan, the crows indeed turned into swans.
Filled with wonder, the local people gathered for the pilgrimage
spoke, pointing with their fingers: 'Ah, look, look!

4.68.s: asmāsu vīkṣamāṇeṣu kākāḥ kuṃḍetra ye patan ..
4.68.d: अस्मासु वीक्षमाणेषु काकाः कुंडेत्र ये पतन् ..
4.68.m: While we were watching, the crows that fell into this pool
have become white swans by the power of this sacred ford!'
From that time onwards, near Kṛttivāsa,
that pool became known in the world by the name Haṃsatīrtha, O jar-born [Agastya]!
Those whose souls are extremely defiled by greatly defiling deeds,
having offered water at Haṃsatīrtha, instantly attain purity.
One should always dwell in Kāśī; one should bathe at Haṃsatīrtha;
one should view Kṛttivāseśa; one shall attain the supreme state.
In Kāśī, O sage, there are many liṅgas at every step;
the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga is considered the head of all liṅgas.
Having worshipped Kṛttivāsa with a heart full of devotion,
the fruit born of worshipping all liṅgas is obtained in Kāśī.
Silent recitation, gifts, austerity, fire oblations, water libations, and the worship of deities—
all performed in the vicinity of Kṛttivāsa becomes endless.
Indeed, this sacred ford is eternally established, O jar-born one,
and it reappeared through the presence of the god, the Great Lord.
These perfected liṅgas remain concealed age after age;
obtaining the presence of Śambhu, they indeed appear again.
Around Haṃsatīrtha, O sage, there are ten thousand
plus two hundred liṅgas consecrated by excellent sages.
Every single one of them grants accomplishment to men dwelling in Avimukta,
the liṅgas beginning with Kātyāyaneśa and ending with Cyavaneśa.
Lomaśeśa is a great liṅga consecrated by Lomaśa;
it is to the west of Kṛttivāsa—having seen it, where is the fear of Death?
Mālatīśa is an auspicious, great liṅga to the north of Kṛttivāsa;
by worshipping that liṅga, a king becomes a lord of elephants.
And the liṅga named Antakeśvara is situated in the north-eastern direction;
even one who has committed great sins becomes free of sin from gazing upon it.
Nearby is the great liṅga Janakeśa, the supreme bestower of knowledge;
from the worship of that liṅga, knowledge of Brahman is obtained.
To its north is the great-formed Asitāṅga Bhairava;
from seeing him, men will have no sight of Yama.
And there is the goddess Śuṣkodarī of fierce eyes,
to the north of Kṛttivāsa, the devourer of obstacles in Kāśī.
To the south-west of that goddess is the vetāla Agnijihva;
when worshipped on a Tuesday, he grants desired accomplishment.
There is the pool Vetālakuṇḍa, which destroys all diseases;
from contact with the water of that pool, the affliction of ulcers and boils disappears.
Having bathed well in Vetālakuṇḍa and having bowed to the vetāla,
one attains the desired accomplishment that is hard to obtain for all embodied beings.
There is a gaṇa with two arms, four feet, and five heads;
from the mere sight of him, sin departs a thousandfold.
To the north of it, O sage, is a fearsome four-horned Rudra;

4.68.s: tripādastu dviśīrṣā ca hastāḥ syuḥ sapta eva hi ...77 ..
4.68.d: त्रिपादस्तु द्विशीर्षा च हस्ताः स्युः सप्त एव हि ...77 ..
4.68.m: he has three feet, two heads, and seven hands.
He roars loudly, in the form of a bull, bound threefold, O jar-born one!

4.68.s: kāśīvighrakarā ye ca ye kāśyāṃ pāpabuddhayaḥ .. 78 ..
4.68.d: काशीविघ्रकरा ये च ये काश्यां पापबुद्धयः .. 78 ..
4.68.m: [He says:] 'Those who create obstacles in Kāśī and those who are evil-minded in Kāśī,
to cut them down, I hold an axe.

4.68.s: ye kāśyāṃ vighnahartāro ye kāśyāṃ dharmabuddhayaḥ .. 79 ..
4.68.d: ये काश्यां विघ्नहर्तारो ये काश्यां धर्मबुद्धयः .. 79 ..
4.68.m: Those who remove obstacles in Kāśī and those who are righteous-minded in Kāśī,
holding a pot of nectar in my hand, I sprinkle their lineage.'

4.68.s: taṃ dṛṣṭvā vṛṣarudraṃ vai pūjayitvā tu bhaktitaḥ .. 4.2.68.80 ..
4.68.d: तं दृष्ट्वा वृषरुद्रं वै पूजयित्वा तु भक्तितः .. 4.2.68.80 ..
4.68.m: Having seen that Bull-Rudra and having worshipped him with devotion
with the grandest offerings of a festival, one is not overcome by obstacles.
To the north of that Rudra there is the serpent named Maṇipradīpa;
and before him is the Maṇikuṇḍa, which supremely removes poisons and diseases.
One who takes a bath in that pool and beholds that serpent
obtains a kingdom filled with gems and rubies, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
and prospering with jewels among women and jewels among sons.
Those by whom the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga has not been seen in Kāśī

4.68.s: te martyaloke bhārāya bhuvo bhūtā na saṃśayaḥ .. 84 ..
4.68.d: ते मर्त्यलोके भाराय भुवो भूता न संशयः .. 84 ..
4.68.m: have undoubtedly become a burden to the earth in the world of mortals.
Skanda said:
Those men who hear of the origin of Kṛttivāsa here
will attain the auspicious fruit resulting from the darśana of that liṅga; there is no doubt about this.

4.68.s: iti śrīskāṃde mahāpurāṇa ekāśītisāhasryāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ caturthe kāśīkhaṃḍa uttarādheṃ kṛttivāsaḥ samudbhavo nāmāṣṭaṣaṣṭitamo'pyāyaḥ ..68..
4.68.d: इति श्रीस्कांदे महापुराण एकाशीतिसाहस्र्यां संहितायां चतुर्थे काशीखंड उत्तराधें कृत्तिवासः समुद्भवो नामाष्टषष्टितमोऽप्यायः ..68..
4.68.m: Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, named 'The Origin of Kṛttivāsa,' in the second half of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa, in the fourth section of the glorious Skandamahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
